The unadapted text disaster
A classroom story in six panels.

Panel 1 of 6

Every good text starts somewhere. But sometimes the version you find online was written for a different time, a different place, and different kids. This is what happens when a text lands in the wrong classroom.

1 / 6
Question 1 of 4
How could AI have helped Ms Nguyen before she gave the text to her class?
Question 2 of 4
Two students mentioned that their families use WeChat and video calls to stay in touch with relatives overseas. How could Ms Nguyen use this in an AI prompt?
Question 3 of 4
If you were planning how to use AI to adapt a text for your own class, which of these would you keep in mind? Select all that apply.
🧠
Teacher expertise goes in first
The teacher identifies what needs changing: local classroom details are not something AI can know without being told.
🤖
Skip teacher input entirely
AI can help flag content that looks outdated, but it does not know your students' specific context, like which apps or technologies their families actually use. That detail still needs to come from you.
🎯
Targeted changes only
A good text only needs specific elements updated, not a complete rewrite. The language level and structure stay the same.
👥
Community and cultural context
References should reflect the actual world of your learners: their technology, their locations, their family structures.
📝
Always start from scratch
It is more reliable to ask the AI to write a completely new text than to adapt an existing one.
✅
Review before it reaches students
The teacher checks the output for accuracy, cultural appropriateness, and pedagogical fit before using it in class.

Why text adaptation matters
1
Teacher expertise is what makes adaptation real
The WeChat detail, the local references, the knowledge of how this community lives, that comes from you, not the AI. It has to go into the prompt.
2
Adapt, do not replace
Ms Nguyen's text was good. The language level, the topic, the structure: all fine. Only the specific references needed updating. That is what adaptation means.
3
Always review before it reaches students
AI does the rewriting. You check whether the output is culturally appropriate, pedagogically sound, and accurate for your learners before it goes anywhere near them.
4
Start with what you know, then prompt AI
Before you open an AI tool, identify what actually needs to change and why. That first step belongs to you: it is what makes the AI's output useful.
